items.title: Ray Brown interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, AZ, April 16, 2000
items.q: Herb Ellis and myself and Buddy Rich or Louis Bellson... Herb Ellis on guitar; Oscar Peterson on piano; Ray Brown on bass

ctx.x: Norman Granz was a pretty important figure in jazz during those years. Was he a pretty upright guy to work for?

Oh yeah. You know he did a lot of brilliant things. First of all he put jazz into the concert hall. He took it out of the dance hall and put it in the concert hall. He took it out of the night club and put it in the concert hall. He gave people the very best musicians, I mean he got the top people, he always had top people playing for him, and he paid top salaries. I mean he was a tough guy. I remember we would finish a tour and it would be, we’d go in the studio and it would be Coleman Hawkins, Lester Young, Ben…

items.title: Herb Ellis interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: I have it with Ray Brown to a great extent. We love to play together.

ctx.x: Can you tell us other musicians that you’ve had that chemistry with?

Oh let me see. Well there’s a lot of them. I had it with Sweets Edison, he’s here at the festival, you know. And I have it with Jake Hanna, the drummer. And of course I have it with Ray Brown to a great extent. We love to play together. So there could be more but I can’t name them all.
Could you also explain to guitarists how that it takes an impeccable sense of time to play in a trio with no drums.

items.title: Herb Ellis interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 16, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: I think certainly playing with Oscar and Ray was a highlight.

ctx.x: Can you recall some of the things.

I can recall one of the things I did. We were playing, whatever place, and we had an intermission. So Oscar had been pulling jokes on Ray and I so I thought I’ll get back at him. So I took tape and taped some of the notes together, under the little lip of the notes, so you can’t see any tape.
